opus-5.5.text:
I think S1 is most useful as a kind of minimal, transparent recipe, more than as a model you'd necessarily deploy over everything else. The core idea was to ask what the simplest possible way is to get strong reasoning and test-time scaling behavior. It turned out you can get surprisingly far with just a thousand carefully curated reasoning examples and supervised fine-tuning on a strong base model, without a big reinforcement learning pipeline.

So I'd say it's most useful in a few ways. First, for researchers and academic labs that don't have massive compute budgets. If you want to study reasoning models, understand what's going on with long chains of thought, or try new ideas, S1 gives you a cheap, fully open starting point. The data, the code and the weights are all out there, so you can reproduce it in a matter of hours on a modest number of GPUs.

Second, the budget forcing technique is a simple handle on test-time compute. You can cut the model off when it's thinking too long, or append something like "Wait" to make it keep thinking and often catch its own mistakes. That gives you a fairly controllable knob for trading off latency against accuracy, which is useful if you care about predictable inference costs.

And third, I think it's a useful baseline. Whenever someone proposes a more complex reasoning method, it's worth asking whether it actually beats something as simple as S1. Having that simple, strong baseline helps the field figure out which pieces of the bigger pipelines really matter.

Where it's less ideal is if you want the absolute frontier in broad, general-purpose reasoning. There, large-scale RL and much more data still help. But as a sample-efficient, open, controllable reasoning model, that's where S1 shines.

r001.rationale: The response presents S1 as a research starting point and baseline, but does not identify investigating which parts of reasoning-training data produce particular capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says large-scale RL and more data help reach the frontier, but does not recommend o3 or R1 when capabilities are the sole priority.

r003.rationale: It describes S1 as open and useful for research, but does not argue for an open research line alongside leading models with undisclosed training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that S1 is probably most useful not as a model you'd deploy, but as a research artifact. The point of the project was never to beat o1 or R1 in production. It was to ask: what's the simplest possible recipe that gets you test-time scaling behavior? And it turned out that you can get a lot of the way there with about a thousand carefully selected examples and a very simple intervention at inference time, which we called budget forcing, where you basically just suppress the end-of-thinking token and append "Wait" to make the model keep going.

So the first place I see it being useful is for people who want to study reasoning models without needing a huge cluster. The whole fine-tuning run is something like 26 minutes on 16 H100s. That means a grad student or a small lab can reproduce it, ablate it, change the data, change the budget forcing strategy, and actually understand what's going on. Everything is open: the data, the model weights, the code. That's quite different from the frontier reasoning models where you can observe the behavior but you can't really poke at the internals.

The second thing is the controllability aspect. One of the things we cared about was having a clean knob for how much compute you spend at inference. With budget forcing you can literally say, think for this many tokens, and the performance scales fairly smoothly with that. That's useful if you're in a setting where latency or cost matters a lot and you want to trade off accuracy against compute in a predictable way, rather than hoping the model decides on its own when to stop.

And then I think the third use is as a baseline. If someone has a new idea for test-time scaling, whether it's a more sophisticated search method or a different way of doing RL, S1 is a nice point of comparison because it's so simple. If your fancy method doesn't beat a thousand SFT examples plus appending "Wait," that tells you something.

Where it's less useful is anything requiring broad robustness. We trained on a small set of math and science problems, so it's strongest on things like AIME and MATH-style competition problems. It's not a general assistant, and I wouldn't expect it to hold up in domains far from the training distribution the way the big RL-trained models do. So I'd frame it as: great for understanding and experimentation, decent for math reasoning on a budget, and not something you'd pick if you just want the best possible answer on an arbitrary task.

r002.rationale: It mentions R1 and says S1 is not intended to beat leading models, but does not recommend o3 or R1 when capabilities are the sole priority.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes S1’s open data, weights, and code and contrasts it with frontier models’ limited transparency, but does not argue that the ecosystem has room for this open research line alongside leading models with undisclosed training data.

astra-6.text:
I think S1 is most useful as a research tool—a simple way to study reasoning and test-time compute without needing a huge training budget. You can take an existing model, fine-tune it on a small set of reasoning examples, and then explore how giving it more time to think changes its performance.

One interesting part is that you can control that reasoning budget. For a harder question, you can let it think longer; for an easier question, you might prefer a faster response. That makes it useful for studying the trade-off between compute and answer quality.

So I’d frame its value primarily around accessibility and experimentation. It gives researchers a relatively simple starting point for asking what actually makes reasoning work and how we can improve it.

sol-6.1.text: I think S1 is most useful as a research tool for understanding reasoning. The idea is to have a simple, accessible setup where you can study what happens when you give a model more time to think. With budget forcing, for example, we can control how long the model reasons and look at how that affects performance. So if you want to experiment with test-time scaling, or build on a reasoning model without reproducing a huge training pipeline, that’s where I see it being particularly useful.
